newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to cut drug prices by 3 percent in April.
newsitem.headline: Japan to cut drug prices by 3 percent in April.

text.p: The Japanese government unveiled a plan on Friday to reduce the official price hospitals pay for drugs from April, a move analysts said could cut deeply into the profitability of some pharmaceutical firms.
The Ministry of Health and Welfare announced it would cut prices under the National Health Insurance system by an average of three percent in April.

"The price cut's impact on the drug industry will be very large, considering drug prices were cut by an average of 6.8 percent only a year ago," said Takeshi Bito, managing director of the Japan Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association.
Pharmaceutical makers usually sell drugs to hospitals at below government-set rates, allowing them to profit from the difference.

Keen to rein in medical spending due to tight budgetary conditions, the government set rules in 1987 under which it reviews drug prices in the government insurance system every two years to ensure the reimbursement rates better reflect actual prices at which hospitals buy medication.
The ministry official also said prices of 7,718 drugs out of the total of 11,974 items listed in the government health insurance system would be cut.
Drug makers will now be forced to review their marketing strategies for hospitals, which are likely to demand reductions in market prices to compensate for the lower reimbursements.
Companies which decide to maintain their prices may face a decline in orders, analysts said.
A Reuters poll on Friday showed that Japanese pharmaceutical makers on average plan to match the official drug price cut of three percent.

"It is becoming increasingly difficult for some drug firms to take such price cuts as they lack new blockbuster drugs to maintain profitability," said Yasuhiro Nakazawa, analyst at Nikko Research Center.
In contrast, firms such as Sankyo Co Ltd which recently launched a new diabetes drug, Noscal, in Japan, may survive better in the face of price cut pressures, he said.
